newsitem.title: UK: Institutional investors not short-termist - study.
newsitem.headline: Institutional investors not short-termist - study.

text.p: Institutional investors are not short-termist and a typical large pension fund may hold shares in the same companies for an average of up to 18 years, performance measurement consultancy WM Company said.
In a study of pension fund investment holdings, WM said high turnover levels in large funds did not necessarily mean funds were holding shares for only short periods.

"The vast majority of their investment is in stocks which they hold long-term. They do make shorter-term tactical judgements on the market value of their investments and act accordingly but that is precisely what an efficient capital market should be doing," said WM research and consultancy director Gordon Bagot.
The study said two-thirds of the value of a typical large fund is traded annually, implying that one-third is bought and one-third sold each year.

"This may imply that funds only hold shares for around three years on average. However, more detailed analysis of trading activity shows that the turnover figure in isolation is highly misleading," Bagot said.
The study said that around two-thirds of turnover is tactical adjustment to long-term holdings and does not represent major moves out of individual stocks.

In one fund, it said a holding in Glaxo was increased and later reduced. The trading generated 32 million sterling of turnover, but the nine million shares held at the end of the period also indicated a long-term commitment to investing in the company.
It said more than half of the remaining turnover was due to involuntary sales, often as a result of acquisitions.

"This means that voluntary sales of complete holdings represent only 8.25 percent of the typical large fund's trading -- equivalent to 5.5 percent of the fund's total value. These figures suggest that large funds typically hold individual stocks for around 18 years on average."
It said small funds were no more active than large funds in total turnover, but they were more likely to trade complete holdings. As a result their average holding period is about eight years.
The study was based on analysis of two representative pension funds with UK equity holdings of 4.5 billion sterling and 20 million respectively.
